outcome: Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved the Kakeya conjecture in the n=3 case (every Kakeya set in R^3 has Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension 3), settling that case while the conjecture as stated (for general n) remains open for n>3.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet as frozen on 26 January 2024 asks whether n-dimensional sets containing a unit line segment in every direction (Kakeya sets) must have Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension equal to n, for general n. On 24 February 2025, Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl posted a 127-page preprint (arXiv:2502.17655, 'Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions') proving this for n=3: every Kakeya set in R^3 has both Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension exactly 3. This settles a specific case (restriction to n=3) of the general conjecture, which is the textbook example of §3.1's 'case of the problem' (dimension is restricted, not the question changed), so I classify it as `partial` rather than `resolved` for the conjecture as stated, even though the n=3 case itself is fully resolved and expert-digested. The proof has been extensively vetted: Terence Tao wrote a detailed technical blog post the same day walking through the strategy (terrytao.wordpress.com, 2025-02-25), Quanta Magazine covered it as a major breakthrough with commentary from Nets Katz calling it 'a once-in-a-century kind of result' (2025-03-14), Larry Guth wrote two survey/exposition papers on the proof (arXiv:2505.07695, arXiv:2604.03416, the latter a Séminaire Bourbaki survey), and — most decisively — Hong Wang was awarded the 2026 Fields Medal explicitly citing 'the proof of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture' as a key contribution, per the IMU citation reflected on her Wikipedia page. This amounts to full expert digestion of the n=3 case. The general conjecture for n>3 remains open; Wikipedia's own Kakeya set article confirms 'the conjecture remains open for n>3,' with partial lower-bound results (e.g., Wolff's bound, Katz-Zahl's planebrush bound of ~3.059 in R^4) but no full resolution. I found no evidence of any AI system involved anywhere in this line of work: the arXiv abstract, Tao's post, Quanta's article, and Guth's surveys contain no mention of AI, machine learning, or computer-assisted proof techniques — this is traditional human mathematical proof via multiscale/convex-geometry arguments building on Wang-Zahl's earlier 2022 'sticky Kakeya sets' work. I also checked the related but distinct 'arithmetic Kakeya conjecture' (an additive-combinatorics reformulation that implies the geometric conjecture, discussed on Epoch AI's FrontierMath open-problems page) — this is a variant/different formulation, not the bullet as stated, and in any case no AI progress on it was reported; Epoch AI lists it as an open research target, not a solved problem, with current best partial result (Katz-Tao, human work) unchanged.
competing_reading: One could argue the n=3 case, being a fully complete and celebrated resolution (Fields Medal-cited), deserves to be read as close to 'resolved' in spirit even though the bullet is about all n. But per §3.1 and §6.1, `resolved` must mean the problem as stated is settled; since the bullet is explicitly the general n-dimensional question and higher dimensions remain open, `partial` is the correct code, with the direction (`confirmed`) describing the settled n=3 piece.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of the Kakeya conjecture for general n (or at least n=4 and beyond) would move this further; short of that, `partial` with direction `confirmed` for the n=3 case is the correct terminal classification barring new work on higher dimensions.
